articles.title: Falling short: on Marco Rubio’s second visit to India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India , his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections , which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement , reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India , gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

articles.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. articles.title: Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

fullParagraphs: The Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC) has forecast heavy to very heavy rain at isolated places in Pudukottai, Sivaganga, and Ramanathapuram districts on Monday.

Heavy rain is likely to occur over isolated places in Kanniyakumari, Tirunelveli, Thoothukudi, Tenkasi, Virudhunagar, Madurai, Theni, Dindigul, Karur, Tiruchi, Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, and Nagapattinam districts.

The remaining parts of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, and Karaikal are likely to witness moderate rain with thunderstorms and lightning at many places. Several areas are likely to witness gusty winds during the thunderstorms, at speeds reaching 40 kmph to 50 kmph.

On Tuesday, isolated places in Ramanathapuram district are likely to get heavy rain. A few places over the rest of south Tamil Nadu and the Western Ghat districts are likely to get moderate rainfall with thunderstorms and lightning. The other areas of the State, Puducherry, and Karaikal are likely to get light rain in a few places.

The deep depression over east-central and adjoining Southeast Bay of Bengal moved westwards and lay centred about 450 km north-northwest of Sri Vijaya Puram (Andaman Islands), 820 km east-southeast of Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), 910 km east-southeast of Kakinada (Andhra Pradesh), 1,010 km east-southeast of Machilipatnam (Andhra Pradesh), and 1,080 km east of Bapatla (Andhra Pradesh), at 5.30 p.m.

It is likely to move westwards and intensify further into a cyclonic storm over east-central and adjoining Southeast Bay of Bengal by early Monday morning. It is then likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over west-central Bay of Bengal by Tuesday morning.

Thereafter, it is likely to move northwestwards, intensify further into a very severe cyclonic storm and reach Westcentral Bay of Bengal near the Andhra Pradesh coast on October 28 morning. It is likely to cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam as a very severe cyclonic storm, with a maximum sustained wind speed of 115-125 kmph, gusting to 140 kmph, by the forenoon of October 28.

Nadda.

He said that in a democracy, opponents must not “cross the bounds of propriety”, and the people will respond to such politics. “The Congress must realise that the trust of the people cannot be won through a politics of hatred and humiliation. articles.title: Is Yashwant Varma still a judge?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Parliament is set to take up in the coming Monsoon Session the report of the Committee appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 to investigate charges of misbehaviour against former Judge of the Allahabad and Delhi High Courts, Yashwant Varma, who has since resigned. The allegations against him arise from the discovery in March 2025 of partially burnt currency notes in an outhouse at his official residence. Mystery surrounds his current status and the future course of the pending proceedings in Parliament.

On one hand, three months after his resignation, Mr. Varma continues to be listed by the Allahabad High Court and by the Department of Justice of the Union government as a sitting judge. This has given rise to misgivings about whether his resignation has taken effect or remains subject to acceptance by the President.

On the other, it has been reported that following Mr. Varma’s resignation on April 9, 2026 “with immediate effect”, his status at the Bar was changed to “active” on resumption of practice. Some of his dues and benefits as a sitting judge have reportedly been stopped since the resignation.
(1) Is Mr. Varma’s resignation subject to acceptance by the President?

Our Constitution vests 13 constitutional functionaries with the “power to resign at will”: the power to demit office at a time of their choosing, without their resignation being subject to acceptance by any authority. They may resign merely by writing under their hand addressed to an authority specified in the Constitution. No further action is necessary. Needing no acceptance, the power to resign at will is an essential safeguard for the independence of these offices. It protects incumbents from being forced to work under coercion, contrary to their conscience.

The offices vesting incumbents with this power are: the President; the Vice-President; the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha; judge of the Supreme Court; judge of High Courts; Governors; the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of a State Assembly; the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of a State Legislative Council; and member of Public Service Commissions.

In contrast, Article 101 (3)(b) of the Constitution expressly says that the resignation of Members of Parliament is subject to acceptance by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, as the case may be. Under Article 190(3)(b), the resignations of members of State Legislative Assemblies and Legislative Councils are likewise subject to acceptance by the Speaker or the Chairman.
A five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Union of India vs Gopal Chandra Misra (1978) unanimously reaffirmed the power of Supreme Court and High Court judges to resign at will.

Justice S. Murtaza Fazal Ali dissented from the majority Judges who held that a resigning Judge could choose a future date and withdraw the resignation before that date. But Justice Ali reflected the unanimous view of the Bench that no acceptance was needed for resignation of judges. He wrote categorically that “the effectiveness of the resignation does not depend upon the acceptance of the resignation by the President…the resignation acts ex proprio vigore” (automatically without requiring any external action).

At least 12 High Court judges have resigned since 2017. One Supreme Court judge, Justice Dalveer Bhandari, resigned in 2012 to join the International Court of Justice. Publicly available information suggests that these resignations have been handled in compliance with the law described above, coming into effect as the resigning judge stipulated, without the effectiveness of the resignation being dependent on acceptance by the President or by anyone else.
(2) Can Mr. Varma still be held out as a sitting judge; can he continue to draw the benefits of office?

Since Mr. Varma ceased to be a judge on April 9, describing him after that date as a sitting judge of the Allahabad High Court in the Department of Justice’s list or on the website of the Allahabad High Court is clearly wrong.

articles.title: Ethanol tender sparks feedstock concerns as rice gains ground over maize
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Oil Marketing Companies’ (OMCs) latest ethanol procurement tender for Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2026–27 has triggered concerns among grain-based ethanol producers and sections of the sugar industry over feedstock pricing, allocation priorities and the potential implications for the sector.

The tender sets procurement prices at ₹60.32 a litre for surplus foodgrains (SFG), with a stated cap of 108 crore litres for the first three quarters; ₹64 a litre for damaged foodgrains (DFG); and ₹66 a litre for maize, plus an additional ₹2.79 a litre. While ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses has been excluded, C-heavy molasses-based ethanol remains eligible for procurement.

The Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association (GEMA) has argued that the tender places a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstocks, particularly SFG and DFG, while potentially weakening maize’s role as an industrial feedstock.
The pricing differential has also created uncertainty over how procurement demand will be distributed among the different feedstock categories.

According to industry estimates, DFG-based ethanol allocation during ESY 2025–26 was approximately 60 crore litres. For ESY 2026–27, the industry anticipates that the allocation could exceed 700 crore litres.

C.K. Jain, president of GEMA, said a balanced ethanol policy must support viable production from both maize and rice, with procurement prices reflecting their different cost structures and allocations providing reasonable visibility to producers. He added that the government and OMCs should review the pricing and allocation framework.

GEMA has also questioned whether maize will receive adequate procurement opportunities under the lowest-price-based allocation mechanism. It has called for greater clarity on the methodology for feedstock-wise allocation and the role envisaged for maize in meeting the country’s ethanol requirements.

The Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) has welcomed the exclusion of ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses, arguing that the approach is consistent with the need to safeguard domestic sugar availability amid uncertainty over the forthcoming crop.
C-heavy molasses-based ethanol, it noted, allows sugar mills to continue contributing to the ethanol-blending programme without diverting recoverable sugar.
However, ISMA has raised concerns over the preferential allocation granted to dedicated ethanol plants holding Long-Term Offtake Agreements under the ESY 2026–27 tender.
While the provision is already in place for the current year, its continuation in subsequent years could hurt the sugar industry, the association said.

articles.title: Data suggests broad-based increase in food prices: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: High-frequency data collected by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for October (till 19th), suggest a broad-based increase in food prices, said RBI officials in the October edition of RBI Bulletin, which was released on Friday (October 23, 2026).

“Among cereals, rice and wheat prices continued to increase. Prices of major pulses also went up sequentially. Edible oil prices also recorded a slow and broad-based increase, led by mustard and palm oil,” they wrote in the ‘State of the Economy’ article.
Among vegetables, while potato prices declined and the pace of onion price increases dropped, tomato prices picked up, they added.

Surprisingly, inflation in rural areas has been getting higher than that in urban areas. Inflation stood at 4.9% and 6.1%, respectively, in urban and rural areas in September. In August, urban and rural inflation stood at 4.3% and 5.2% respectively, the officials stated.
ALSO WATCH The battle against inflation is entering a tougher phase: What it means for you

The majority of States/UTs recorded inflation in the range of 4-6% in September. Inflation ranged from 2.9% to 6.9% across states/UTs. States like Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry recorded inflation in excess of 6% across both rural and urban areas, they pointed out.

Stating that WPI inflation recorded its first double-digit rate in the new series (Base 2022-23) at 11.4% in September 2026, rising from 9.9% in August, reflecting a broad-based increase in prices, they said industrial and farm input costs remained elevated.
Inflation in the Output Producer Price Index surged to 11.4% in September 2026 from 9.8% in August, led by manufacturing products, and mining & quarrying, they said.
As per the article headline, CPI inflation edged up over the months and showed signs of greater generalisation across commodities, calling for a commensurate change in the monetary policy stance.
“The external headwinds are also being dealt with a slew of regulatory measures by the Reserve Bank to curb speculative activity in foreign exchange market,” they stated.

“Strong inflows under FCNR(B) swap window augmented reserves. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) and remittance flows strengthened in August. With strong exports growth, the trade deficit narrowed in September,” they added.

The headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rose to a 23-month high of 5.5% (YoY) in September from 4.8% in August, driven by a broad-based increase in food, fuel and core (CPI excluding food and fuel) components.

articles.title: Bharat Petroleum’s net profit dips amid volatile crude prices in Q2
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Bharat Petroleum’s standalone net profits in the September-end quarter fell 22.5% on a year-over-year basis as volatile crude prices impacted margins following the reignited conflict in West Asia.
The Mumbai-headquartered refiner’s net profit declined to ₹4,993.17 crore in the reported quarter compared to ₹6,442.5 crore in the same period last year.
The state-owned oil-marketing company’s cost of materials consumed soared 44.2% during the period to ₹74,969 crore.
Revenues increased about 30% on a year-over-year basis to more than ₹1.58 lakh crore.
The refiners’ physical performance reported an uptick. It rose 6% during the mentioned period to 10.41 million metric tonnes (MMT).
Its peer Hindustan Petroleum had reported a 9% decline in standalone net profits on Thursday.
Delhi-headquartered peer Indian Oil is scheduled to post their September-end financial results on October 30.

articles.title: IndusInd Bank posts profit of ₹1,242 crores in Q2; asset quality improvement and interest income drives growth
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: IndusInd Bank Limited posted a net profit of ₹1,242 crore for the quarter ended September, up 20% sequentially and trimming net loss of ₹437 for the same quarter in the preceding year. The bank had incurred net loss for the same period in previous year due to an increase in microfinance provisioning and write-offs.

The bank’s bottom line for Q2FY27 was supported by a rise in net interest income, which stood at ₹4,569 crore as against ₹4,409 crores a year ago. Sequentially, interest income declined by 2%. NII for half year (H1FY27) rose to ₹9,254, up 2.3% on year.

Asset quality of the bank improved substantially, with gross non-performing assets (NPA) ratio at 2.73% compared to 3.60% on year and net NPA declining to 0.83% from 1.04% in Q2FY26. However, the net interest margin of the bank slipped to 3.23% from 3.32% a year ago.

Net revenue of the bank for the period rose to ₹6,817 crores compared to ₹6,00 crores a year. A decline in operating expenses also helped push the bottom-line numbers, with expenses slipping to ₹3,943 crores in July-Septemeber from ₹4,013 crore for the same period last year.
Deposits of the bank rose 10% year-on-year to ₹4.28 crores. Advances of the bank for the period stood at 3.63 crores.
IndusInd held provisions of $9,012 crore as of September 30, with the provision coverage ratio at 70%.

IndusInd Bank raised nearly $3.5 billion via the Reserve Bank of India’s special window for foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR-B) account, which was impacted the contraction in NIM. The bank said recovery in margin related to FCNR-B is expected over the next two quarters.

“Q2 reflects the growing strength of the IndusInd Bank franchise and the progress we have made in rebuilding momentum across the business. Our Q2 results demonstrate that the growth has strengthened, profitability has improved, asset quality trends remain encouraging, and our funding profile is becoming more granular and resilient,” Rajiv Anand, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of IndusInd Bank said.

The bank also informed the exchanges on Friday (October 23, 2026) that the Board of Directors of the lender has appointed Priyanka Sinha as an Additional Director in the category of Non-Executive Independent Director for a period of four consecutive years, till October 22, 2030.

Speaking to the media at post-earnings conference call, the bank said it remains confident of reaching a 1% exit return on assets for FY27. Bank also expects loans growth momentum to continue driven by retail and wholesale lending. Shares of IndusInd Bank Ltd closed at ₹835.00 on Friday, down 1.76%, on the BSE.

fullParagraphs: The Union government has decided to change the design and structure of the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) to track digital platform workers and capture engagement in unpaid household, caregiving, volunteer, and trainee work. The PLFS will also include additional questions to measure labour underutilisation.

According to a press release and concept note issued in New Delhi on Friday (October 23, 2026), the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), has proposed modifications to the PLFS sampling design starting January 2027. The survey schedule will also change.
The Ministry has invited comments and suggestions from policymakers, researchers, academic institutions, and the public within 15 days from Friday.

A separate Second Stage Stratum (SSS) will be introduced in the PLFS to identify households with at least one digital platform worker. An additional entry will be added to the questionnaire to determine whether any member of the household has engaged in digital platform work during the specified reference period.

“There will be four SSSs in rural areas and five in urban areas, with 14 households canvassed in each selected First Stage Unit (FSU). This revision in SSS formation is expected to improve the coverage of digital platform workers and facilitate more comprehensive data collection on this emerging segment of the labour market,” the press release said.

According to the concept note, a large proportion of women in India spend considerable time on unpaid household and caregiving activities, such as cooking, cleaning, childcare, and caring for elderly, sick, or disabled family members. “While such activities contribute significantly to household well-being and facilitate the participation of other household members in paid employment, they have not been measured separately in PLFS until now,” it noted, adding that specific questions will be incorporated to capture engagement in own-use production of goods, unpaid household and caregiving activities, volunteer work, and unpaid trainee work.

Additionally, the criteria for sample allocation and stratification have been updated based on the experience of the previous two years. “These revisions are expected to improve the efficiency of sample allocation and stratification and ensure better representation of population variations, which in turn will minimise operational difficulties during sample selection,” the press release said.

articles.title: Crude oil sourcing presently volatile; procuring more on landed basis: HPCL Chief
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Crude oil sourcing at present is very volatile and unpredictable, and Hindustan Petroleum is procuring more on a delivered basis than free-on-board (FOB) and term contracts, Vikas Kaushal, Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) of the state-owned oil-marketing company told analysts in an investor call on Friday (October 23, 2026).
Purchases on delivered basis entail the seller bearing the cost of shipping the oil and associated risks until it reaches the buyer’s port or facility.

“All I can say if you look at crude premiums and landed cost: there are times when there are premiums and there are times when you can even pick it up at discounts. It is a very ‘Wild West’ right now” he said.
Separately, Mr. Kaushal also explained there could be instances of discount though the freights could be very high at that time.
Srividya Venkataraman, Director (Finance) informed analysts that freight costs had doubled between the first quarter and the second quarter.
She observed that shipping costs on a Suezmax tanker moved up to $9 per barrel from around $4 per barrel in June.
Though, Mr. Kaushal also stated that landed price may not be as high as it may appear.

“The producers of oil are also stuck. Thus, the astronomical freight rates that you see: if you strike a good deal, you can get is almost managed on the producer,” he explained, adding, “So, the net back to producers in many situations, especially those who are stuck or where there is stranded oil right now, the net backs are much lower than what is in the public domain.”

The HPCL chief also told analysts that the company is procuring more on landed basis expect in cases where sending a ship is cheaper. He added this is also to avert the probability of a ship being attacked enroute.
Ms. Venkataraman informed that under-recoveries on liquified petroleum gas (LPG) stood at ₹245 per cylinder in October and is projected at ₹327 per cylinder in November.
She added that the total under-recovery for LPG in the September-end quarter stood at ₹500 crores.

Separately, Mr. Kaushal also informed analysts that Hindustan Petroleum has petrol and diesel stocks combined for twenty days. This excludes the crude that is presently being processed in their refineries.

articles.title: Behind China’s AI gift, a constraint
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: At the ninth World AI Conference in Shanghai this month, Chinese President Xi Jinping addressed the gathering for the first time in nine years. It is indicative of the priority that AI occupies for the leadership. At the conference, Mr. Xi pitched Chinese AI models as a global public good. The contrast was clear as day. America is selling closed-source, proprietary models while China is offering open-weight models to the world. This distinction is not merely technical, but equally political.

Unlike Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, which host their frontier models on their respective servers and offer services via an application programming interface (API), Chinese labs such as DeepSeek, Qwen, and Moonshot also release their weights for anyone to download. Unlike American models, these can be customised, modified, and even further trained. There is no subscription to cancel or terms of service. The maker cannot revoke or restrict access. So long as one can manage the requisite compute to host the model, even Papua New Guinea or Senegal can run it locally on their servers. And most importantly, the data never leaves the border.

However, one may wonder what explains China’s benevolence. Well, to begin with, the objective is to project China as a responsible AI player in the comity of nations. Unlike the Americans, who he alleged to have overstretched the concept of national security to AI, and thereby adopted an exclusionary approach, China is committed to sharing the benefits and fruits of AI. Mr. Xi’s framing was indicative in this regard. He described AI as “humanity’s collective wisdom,” a “historic opportunity” to “bridge the AI and digital divides,” and something that “should not be a solo performance by a single country but a symphony of international cooperation.” The underlying message, aimed at Washington, projected Beijing as the open and cooperative alternative to the U.S.’s AI models.
But there is a limiting factor at play too that explains Beijing’s benevolence — its compute constraint, both for training and inference.
Since 2022, the U.S. administration, in concert with its allies, has imposed a series of export restrictions on China, limiting its ability to both mass-import and mass-manufacture high-end chips.

To understand this constraint, one must separate two very different tasks — training a model and serving it. Training is a one-time cost. A lab assembles a cluster of chips, runs it for a few months and comes up with a finished model. The fleet required is numerically small. For instance, GPT-4 was trained on an estimated 25,000 Nvidia chips, and Meta trained its Llama 3.1 on ~16,400 chips. DeepSeek, on the other hand, trained its acclaimed V3 model on ~2,000 export-compliant H800s. A frontier model, in other words, needs chips in the thousands, and it needs them only once.

Serving that model to the public, however, is an altogether different proposition. Inference scales with the user base and requires continuous expansion as it must answer hundreds of millions of user queries. OpenAI crossed a million GPUs in 2025, and Meta targeted the equivalent of 1.3 million by the end of 2025. Thus, for any model with a mass consumer base, the serving fleet dwarfs the training fleet, often by ten to a hundred times.

In other words, the distinction is that of a stockpile and a flow. To train a model, a lab can accumulate ten or twenty thousand chips through smuggling, stockpiling, and modest domestic production. This is precisely why the export controls could not prevent China from reaching parity at the model level. Inference, however, cannot be solved this way. The export controls mean that the most advanced chips remain out of bounds for Chinese firms. Additionally, the concessions the U.S. has offered exist largely on paper. Around 10 Chinese firms were cleared in principle to buy up to 75,000 H200 chips each, but not a single unit had been delivered by mid-2026, as sales remained stalled and Beijing itself directed firms towards domestic alternatives.

China can attempt to bridge the shortfall through domestic production, but even here, restrictions on export of EUVs continue to prove a handicap. SMIC’s 5nm line in China runs at roughly 20% yield without EUV tools, far short of commercial viability. This severely restricts the ability of Chinese labs to offer services via API alone. DeepSeek’s decision to freeze new registrations in January 2025 was influenced by a surge in traffic it could not serve, alongside a reported ‘large-scale malicious attack’.

Furthermore, given that Chinese models are nearly as good as the U.S.’s frontier models, their popularity is increasing. Data show that the Chinese models’ share of U.S. firms’ AI usage has hit a record 60% on OpenRouter — a marketplace for routing queries to various models based on requests.

American firms are preferring Chinese models as they provide comparable services at a fraction of the cost. But this success comes with a rider — the need for enormous compute. The solution thus is to simply outsource compute via open-weight models. Hence, China’s open-weight offering to the world is largely a product of its structural constraint. It can build models that rival the U.S. but cannot serve them at scale.

But Beijing cannot ignore the urge to securitise and restrain access for too long. Sooner or later, it will face that choice. Indeed, Beijing is already reported to be weighing restrictions on overseas access to its most capable models.

articles.title: Israel presses ahead with West Bank operation as election approaches
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The Israeli military pressed ahead on Sunday (October 25, 2026) with a massive military operation in the occupied West Bank that has displaced hundreds of Palestinians and placed major restrictions on movement in response to a gun attack last week that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others.

The operation, focused on the city of Hebron, the site of Friday’s attack, came as Israel enters the final days before a tense election, which is largely seen as a referendum on current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership and security policies during the past three years of war.

In new measures, the Army said that most Palestinian workers with permits will not be allowed to enter Israeli West Bank settlements on Sunday and Monday, and crossings into Israel will remain closed until after Israel’s elections on Tuesday.

The military said it operated in more than 400 different locations over the weekend and arrested 40 Palestinians it claimed were affiliated with the Hamas or Islamic Jihad militant groups. No militant group has taken responsibility for the attack.
The Hebron municipality said the operation displaced more than 2,600 people.

The military said that troops were conducting searches in the area where the gunmen operated, and warned residents to evacuate Deir Bahha, the suspected gunmen’s neighborhood. After Friday’s attack, Israel’s military said it found weapons in the gunmen’s car and that they were likely planning to attack Israeli civilians before being stopped at the checkpoint where the shootout erupted.
All entrances and exits to the city remained sealed, with the operation focused in Deir Bahha and another part of the city called Al-Jalda, according to Hebron Mayor Yousef Zuhair Al-Jabari.

“People cannot reach or enter the city, and they cannot leave it. The blockade has affected every aspect of life,” Mr. Al-Jabari said. He added that the blockade is forcing businesses to close and has also shuttered a mosque.

“The army told us that this area would be closed for 12 days. Now they’re saying 12 days, but maybe they’ll leave the area after two or three days,” said Shadi al-Qawasmi, a Hebron resident who was displaced with his family. “This may be because of the elections or some political matter. No one knows except God Almighty.”
The Army declined to say how long the operation might last.
ALSO WATCH Israel launches multi-day operation in occupied West Bank after 2 soldiers killed

The operation forced some families to leave the city on foot. At some military gates, people passed sacks of flour and gas canisters through the gates, while an elderly man pushed his wife in a wheelchair through an opening beside one of them. Another family attempted to navigate the gate to access medical appointments.

articles.title: Starshield | The non-state sovereigns
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: On October 14, Ukrainian soldiers using drones to attack Russian forces in Zaporizhzhia and elsewhere started to find many of their machines were losing satellite connectivity. Given Ukraine’s extensive and largely successful use of drones in the war, the anomaly was noticeable, forcing operators to abandon missions.

Experts later traced the problem to a satellite communications service provided by U.S.-based SpaceX, called Starshield. A week later, The Wall Street Journal reported the disruption had been deliberate: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had personally asked for the connectivity to be throttled. Where the order first originated has been disputed, in Mr. Musk’s office or in the White House. But wherever it did, the fact remains: Mr. Musk was able to take para-state action in a war between two sovereign countries. (On October 22, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had asked Mr. Musk to restore connectivity.)

SpaceX’s Starlink satellite constellation currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites in low-earth orbit that provide Internet connectivity to users on the ground. Starshield uses the same constellation to provide secure communications important to national security, with stronger data encryption; its other services, including remote-sensing, use specialised satellites. Ukraine uses Starshield because Russia’s invasion in early 2022 has damaged the eastern European nation’s telecom infrastructure.

By December 2024, the Pentagon had also arranged for Ukraine to access Starshield through roughly 3,000 terminals. Today, its forces use the service to track enemy positions and supply routes and to intercept drones, with the Starlink satellites relaying information.

Mr. Trump has been insisting Ukraine stop attacking Russia’s oil refineries over his worries about surging international oil prices, primed by his war in West Asia. When Mr. Trump objected once more on October 10, Mr. Musk chipped in that Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had gone too far. Four days later, Ukrainian soldiers felt the pinch.

For decades now, private contractors have supplied armies with arms, intelligence, and logistical support. However, the armies had physical ownership of and control over many of the weapons they purchased. With Starshield, however, the provider continued to retain the ability to change the operating conditions of the ‘assistance’ even after the customer had begun using it — like a grenade launcher that could launch grenades to 150 m on most days but suddenly launched only to five metres on one, because you were not fighting your war the way the manufacturer preferred.

The existence of such an entity is the basis of Mr. Musk’s parastate power. Ordinarily, the decision to stop or withhold a country’s military operations would involve political leaders and defence officials. Now, however, Starshield has well and truly complicated the relationship between public authority and private ownership. Perhaps it was a matter of time.

In 2022, Mr. Musk refused Ukraine’s request to activate Starlink connectivity near Sevastopol, the largest city in Crimea, which Russia has annexed, to enable Ukrainian forces to target Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. Mr. Musk later expressed some consternation about the conflict escalating — a compunction he seems to have lost since, even as his own relationship with Mr. Trump has soared and plummeted. Nonetheless, the fact that the concerns of a single non-state actor could matter at all — an absurd notion in an earlier era — has become a strategic reality. Subsequent Pentagon contracts have sought, at least in part, to formalise the relationship between Starlink and the U.S. military.

Today’s armies, and their wars, increasingly depend on satellite communications, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence, all of which private contractors can develop and package at speed and deploy at scale. Musk’s actions with Starshield last week have revealed that military action had until recently depended, perhaps passively, on the lack of such speed and scale as one kind of safeguard. Now that their importance is shrinking, armies of the present and future must deliberate on what can replace them.

articles.title: Netanyahu warns Iran may try to disrupt Israel election, says 'don't test us'
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday's (October 27, 2026) Israeli elections, warning the Islamic Republic against any hostile acts.

Mr. Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, touting the war he launched against Iran in February alongside the United States and suggesting that he alone can see it through. "We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections," he said in a video released by his office on Sunday.
"Don't test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows," he added, noting the military was ready for both defensive and offensive operations.

Earlier in the day, the PM posted an AI-generated image of a mushroom cloud engulfing Tel Aviv, alongside text attributed to a right-wing political commentator calling Iran an existential threat and arguing that all the other issues discussed this election season were trivial in comparison.
Mr. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, has focused heavily on hawkish national security statements in the final days of the campaign.

Earlier in the week, he said he had sent a directive to Israel's security forces to topple Iran's clerical state. A day earlier, he posted a video of himself in front of a fighter jet speaking to U.S. President Donald Trump by phone saying they would "finish the job" together.

articles.title: Two Indian-American candidates face key U.S. midterm races as early voting begins
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Indian-American candidates Amish Shah and Pia Dandiya have favourable prospects in their respective races for the U.S. House of Representatives in Arizona and Florida in the midterm elections, according to pre-poll predictions.

Mr. Shah, a 48-year-old physician and former state representative, is in the fray from the First District in Arizona against former National Football League kicker Jay Feely, the Republican candidate who has received an endorsement from President Donald Trump.
Ms. Dandiya, a 39-year-old former high school principal, is contesting from South Florida's 22nd district, which was carved out in redistricting, against Casey Askar of the Republican Party.
Mr. Shah and Ms. Dandiya are contesting key races that are crucial for Democrats to flip the U.S. House in the midterm elections on November 3. Early voting has begun in Arizona and Florida.
President Trump's Republican Party is facing a crucial electoral test against the opposition Democratic Party.

The Cook Political Report, which provides non-partisan analysis of election campaigns, has listed Shah’s election from Arizona’s first Congressional district as “lean Democratic” in the Republican stronghold.
It also lists Ms. Dandiya’s contest from Florida’s newly carved-out 22nd district as a “toss-up”.
Prediction market Kalshi gives an 80% chance of Mr. Shah’s victory against Mr. Feely in Arizona. It has projected a 60% chance of Ms. Dandiya’s win in Florida.

"Jay Feely wants you to believe he's his own man. Meanwhile, Trump and his allies are spending millions to get their golf buddy elected. They know whose side he’s on. I’m running to lower your costs and protect your healthcare. My loyalty is to you,” Mr. Shah said in a post on X.
Mr. Shah is a three-term member of the Arizona House of Representatives and lost the 2024 U.S. Congressional elections to Republican David Schweikert by a margin of 3.8%.
Born and raised in Palm Beach County, Florida, Pia Dandiya started her career as a teacher and was a high school principal in Harlem. (Photo: www.piaforcongress.com)
Ms. Dandiya is running on a platform focused on education and affordability.

articles.title: LS Speaker Om Birla meets counterparts from Cuba, Russia ahead of BRICS parliamentary forum meeting
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Ahead of Cuba’s resolution against the U.S. blockade to be taken up by the UN General Assembly on October 27, the Caribbean nation intensified its diplomatic outreach to the Global South on Sunday (October 25, 2026), with the Vice President of Cuba’s National Assembly of People’s Power and the Council of State Mari Machado meeting Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla here.

Following the meeting with Ms. Machado, Mr. Birla said they had “discussed strengthening parliamentary exchanges, capacity-building and cooperation in healthcare and pharmaceuticals.” Cuba is participating in the BRICS Parliamentary Forum meeting as a partner country of the grouping.

This comes two days after Cuba’s ambassador to India Juan Carlos Marsan Aguilera accused the United States of carrying out a naval blockade that has created an acute energy crisis in his country. “Cuba is fully capable of defending itself. The U.S. is practising the Monroe Doctrine in our region,” Mr. Aguilera said, seeking support for Cuba’s UNGA resolution.

Mr. Birla also met the Chairman of the State Duma of Russia, Vyacheslav Volodin, on Saturday (October 24), to discuss bilateral ties. India and Russia are marking the 80th anniversary of their bilateral relationship and the two dignitaries carried out a review of parliament-level exchanges between the two countries against the backdrop of unfolding global and regional developments.

The Lok Sabha Speaker informed the Russian delegation about the steps taken to make parliamentary proceedings accessible in various Indian languages through Sansad Bhashini. According to a statement issued by the Parliament Secretariat, Mr. Birla highlighted the importance of using technology in making parliamentary functioning more accessible, efficient, and people-centric.

articles.title: How people’s genes are revealing why some languages are so unique
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Hindi and Tamil differ in far more than just vocabulary . Languages differ in how they are organised, and these differences are not spread evenly around the world. In some regions, neighbouring languages like Basque and Spanish differ dramatically from one another. In others, they share many of the same features, like Tamil and Kannada.

A new study by researchers from Europe and Japan has found human history itself gives shape to the pattern. After analysing thousands of languages alongside genetic data from populations around the world, the researchers found that places that were relatively isolated for a long time tended to harbour more linguistic features. On the other hand, regions shaped by migration and sustained contact contained languages that were more alike.

“I was struck by the clarity of the signal,” Anna Graff, lead author of the study and a biological anthropologist at the University of Zurich, said. “In studies of human history and diversity, such clear global patterns are often difficult to find.”

Crucially, the researchers did not count the number of languages in a region. Instead, they measured how different neighbouring languages were from one another. Some languages placed verbs near the beginning of a sentence while others placed them at the end. Some distinguished between a hand and a finger with separate words while others used the same term for both.

A region where languages had more such differences was considered more linguistically diverse than one where languages shared many of the same traits — even if both regions had the same number of languages.

To investigate, the researchers assembled one of the largest datasets of its kind, combining information from more than 4,200 languages with genetic data from over 5,700 individuals representing 650 populations around the world. Then they divided the world into hundreds of roughly 500-km-wide hexagonal cells and calculated two measures for each: diversity of linguistic features found among languages spoken there and the genetic diversity of the local populations.
Thus they found that regions whose populations had been relatively isolated over long periods tended to have more diverse linguistic features.

The effect was modest. Imagine describing each language using a checklist of 333 characteristics. The difference associated with isolation was roughly equivalent to making about 11 items on the checklist vary substantially across the languages spoken in a region.
Yet the pattern proved remarkably persistent, appearing again and again, across statistical tests.

The researchers also tested if the pattern could be explained by other obvious factors. Languages spoken close together often influence one another while related languages can resemble one another because they inherited features from a common ancestor. Yet neither explanation fully accounted for the trend.

At first glance, the findings also seem counterintuitive. One might expect places with a long history of migration and population mixing to have more language patterns. But Dr. Graff and her colleagues argued that contact often has the opposite effect. As people move, trade, and interact, languages can borrow words, sounds, and grammatical features from one another, gradually becoming more alike.
Isolation allows languages to evolve independently, increasing the chances that they will grow more different over time.

articles.title: KSSP supports distribution of generic drug for SMA patients in Keralam

fullParagraphs: The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP) has supported the Kerala Health Department’s decision to provide a low-cost generic version of the drug Risdiplam to patients afflicted with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a rare and threatening genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness.
In a statement, KSSP president C. Ramakrishnan and general secretary V. Manoj Kumar said that access to this medication is crucial for improving the quality of life and life expectancy of patients.
The statement from the pro-Left people’s science movement comes close on the heels of public health experts such as B. Ekbal, K.P. Aravindan, and V. Ramankutty endorsing the government’s stand.

The KSSP functionaries pointed out that Natco Pharma is an Indian pharmaceutical company that plays a key role in making affordable cancer treatments more accessible to the general public, both in India and in international markets. They claimed that the department’s decision is not merely aimed at saving public funds. It is a humanitarian responsibility to ensure that life-saving treatment is accessible to more SMA patients, they added.

articles.title: Science Snapshots: October 25, 2026
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Art historians have debated whether Vincent van Gogh’s ‘The Starry Night’ painting depicts an actual sky. The painting has been dated to mid-June 1889 but the sky then does not match the real sky of that period. Using astronomical simulations, view reconstructions, historical weather data, and Van Gogh’s correspondence, researchers have now found the painting closely matches the dawn sky on around July 22, 1889, with the celestial canvas nearly mirroring Van Gogh’s view from Saint-Rémy.

Why do moderately cold temperatures prolong lifespan? Using the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans , scientists found cold exposure stimulates muscle cells to produce the metabolite BH2, which travels to intestines and neurons, where a salvage enzyme converts it to BH4. BH4 then drives tyrosine synthesis via the enzyme PAH-1, extending lifespan. Boosting BH2 production in muscles alone could extend lifespan. Treating patient-derived motor neurons with BH2 also prevented toxic protein aggregation linked to Huntington’s disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Grouping buildings with similar functions, such as schools and houses, into larger clusters can cool cities, a study has found. Using a metric to measure the continuous size of such clusters in 101 cities, scientists found larger clusters correlate with lower surface heat. Every 100-m increase in cluster scale reduces urban heat island intensity by 4.5% because buildings with similar functions have comparable shapes and operating schedules, allowing for better airflow and coordinated heat release.

articles.title: Fitbit Air Review | Screenless companion for easy health monitoring
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: I remember Fitbit as a slim tracking device worn on the wrist , from a time when fitness bands were about counting steps and monitoring activity, long before the smartwatch craze took over. Over the years, wearables have evolved into mini smartphones, complete with displays, notifications and apps.

With the Fitbit Air, Google brings back some of that original simplicity in a new avatar. Priced at ₹13,999 in India, this screenless tracker focuses on health monitoring, sleep insights and activity tracking, with Google Health and Gemini-powered coaching adding a layer of intelligence. It is designed to stay out of the way while keeping tabs on your health throughout the day.
After spending time with it, the question is whether this return to the basics works for today’s fitness-focused users. Let’s find out.

The Fitbit Air takes a different approach to wearable design by keeping the hardware compact and unobtrusive. The tracking module weighs just 5.2 grams, while the device weighs around 12 grams with its band. It has a small, pebble-shaped sensor housed inside a woven fabric strap, giving it the appearance of a simple wristband rather than a conventional smartwatch. There is no display or physical button, which keeps the design clean and minimal.

Comfort is one of the Fitbit Air’s biggest strengths. Its lightweight construction makes it comfortable to wear throughout the day and while sleeping. The woven band sits gently on the wrist, while its adjustable fastening helps achieve a secure fit for continuous tracking. This matters for a device designed to collect health data around the clock, rather than something you wear only during workouts. The tracker also has a detachable sensor module, allowing you to change bands without replacing the device.

The Fitbit Air has a small status LED that responds to a firm double-tap. A white light indicates sufficient battery, while red signals that the charge is low. It also includes a vibration motor for silent alarms and reminders. The tracker offers water resistance up to 50 metres, making it suitable for swimming, although the fabric band needs proper drying after water exposure. Google offers the tracker in Obsidian, Berry, Lavender and Fog, with interchangeable band options.

The Fitbit Air relies on the Google Health app for almost everything beyond collecting data. Once paired with a smartphone, it tracks activity and health metrics in the background and syncs them to the app. The dashboard brings together steps, sleep, heart rate, readiness and cardio load, making it possible to review daily activity without needing a screen on the wrist.

The app offers plenty of information, although understanding some of the metrics takes time. Its separate sections for Today, Fitness, Sleep and Health make it easier to explore individual readings. You can also connect supported health services and devices. Another useful feature is the ability to keep the Fitbit Air and a Pixel Watch connected to the same account. This works well if you prefer a smartwatch during the day but want a lighter tracker for sleeping.

Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini, is one of the more interesting additions. Available through a Google Health Premium subscription, it interprets health data, suggests workouts, explains recovery scores and helps create personalised fitness plans. Instead of simply presenting numbers, it aims to explain what they mean and how you can act on them. However, some recommendations can feel generic, and the feature needs refinement before its guidance consistently feels personal. It should also be treated as a wellness tool, and not a substitute for medical advice.

Google includes a three-month Premium trial with the Fitbit Air. After that, the subscription costs ₹499 per month or ₹4,999 annually. Basic activity tracking, sleep information and several recovery metrics remain available without a subscription, which means you can continue using the core features without an ongoing payment.

The Fitbit Air’s screenless design makes the experience genuinely distraction-free. You do not have notifications appearing on your wrist or a display encouraging you to check it repeatedly. The tracker collects information quietly, leaving the phone app to handle the analysis. This approach works particularly well for people who want to monitor their health without adding another source of digital interruptions.

Sleep tracking is one of the more detailed parts of the experience. The Fitbit Air automatically detects sleep and daytime naps, so you do not have to start a session manually. During testing, it recorded sleep duration and estimated the time spent in deep, REM and light sleep. It also highlighted periods of restlessness and time spent awake. The presentation makes it easy to see how the night unfolded, although sleep stages remain estimates rather than clinical measurements.

articles.title: Apple bets iPhone Duo can remake foldable market as sales begin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Sales of Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, began on ‌Friday, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market just like ​the iPhone did for smartphones.
The Duo’s reception could prove an early test for new ⁠CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September.
It could also have large implications for a niche category in which rivals such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium offerings for several years.

Within minutes ‌of pre-orders opening last Friday, Apple’s estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response from customers “nothing short of extraordinary.”
In Sydney, the ‌first Apple store to sell the phones on Friday, a queue of customers formed outside before opening ‌at ⁠8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT).
Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer, paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a Duo with 512GB ⁠memory.
“This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it’s so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life’s too short,” he said.

Early reviews have praised the Duo’s design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones ​whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback ‌and potential deterrent for buyers.

But reviewers have said camera compromises including the absence of a telephoto lens and third-party apps that still need to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers. They have also said the Duo in its smaller, folded state is less handy for the litany of quick tasks that ‌most users carry out each day on standard iPhones, with several prominent reviewers recommending against the Duo for ​many Apple customers.

“It’s been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I’ve gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that ⁠I’d want to buy and carry,” longtime Apple commentator John Gruber, author of the blog Daring Fireball, wrote in a review.

Tech commentator Marques Brownlee, popularly known as MKBHD, said in a YouTube review that “if you’re just a regular person who doesn’t ‌do much more than texting, social media and browsing here and there, then it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn’t mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone.”

The limited supplies could disappoint Apple fans lining up in front of stores to buy the Duo. Apple told Reuters that walk-in availability would vary by country, with limited stocks in the US, Australia, Canada, Mexico and much of Britain and Europe. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and ‌Japan, units would be available only for customers who had ordered online.

articles.title: Falling short: on Marco Rubio’s second visit to India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India , his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections , which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement , reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India , gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

articles.title: In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.

articles.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.

articles.title: Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.
